results.title: Infinite groups without nontrivial proper pronormal subgroups (Kourovka 19.74, Revin)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The statement that there is an infinite group $G$ in which every pronormal subgroup is trivial or equal to $G$. Here a subgroup $H$ of $G$ is pronormal when, for every $g \in G$, the subgroups $H$ and $H^g = gHg^{-1}$ are conjugate by an element of $\langle H, H^g \rangle$.

results.title: An infinite group without nontrivial proper pronormal subgroups exists
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There is an infinite group $G$ in which every pronormal subgroup is trivial or equal to $G$. Here a subgroup $H$ of $G$ is pronormal when, for every $g \in G$, the subgroups $H$ and $H^g = gHg^{-1}$ are conjugate by an element of $\langle H, H^g \rangle$. This answers Kourovka Problem 19.74 in the affirmative.

results.title: Stark–Heegner theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $d$ be a positive squarefree integer and let $K$ be a number field of degree $2$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ that contains an element $x$ with $x^2 = -d$, so that $K = \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-d})$. Then $K$ has class number $1$ if and only if $d \in \{1, 2, 3, 7, 11, 19, 43, 67, 163\}$.

results.title: Twice a triangular number
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $a$, $2\binom{a+1}{2} = a(a+1)$.

results.title: Jacobi's cube series
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Jacobi's cube series is the formal power series $J(X) = \sum_{t \ge 0} (-1)^t (2t+1) X^{t(t+1)/2}$ in $\mathbb{Z}[[X]]$: for each natural number $t$ its coefficient at the triangular number $t(t+1)/2$ is $(-1)^t (2t+1)$, and all its other coefficients are $0$.

results.title: Coefficients of Jacobi's cube series at triangular numbers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $J(X)$ be Jacobi's cube series. For every natural number $t$, the coefficient of $X^{t(t+1)/2}$ in $J(X)$ is $(-1)^t (2t+1)$.

results.title: Vanishing coefficients of Jacobi's cube series
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $J(X)$ be Jacobi's cube series. If a natural number $b$ is not of the form $t(t+1)/2$ for any natural number $t$, then the coefficient of $X^b$ in $J(X)$ is $0$.

results.title: Jacobi's cube identity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E(X) = \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} (-1)^k X^{k(3k-1)/2}$ be Euler's pentagonal series and $J(X) = \sum_{t \ge 0} (-1)^t (2t+1) X^{t(t+1)/2}$ Jacobi's cube series, both in $\mathbb{Z}[[X]]$. Then $E(X)^3 = J(X)$.

results.title: Partition congruences from a power of Euler's series
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be a prime, let $r < p$ be a natural number, and let $E(X) = \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} (-1)^k X^{k(3k-1)/2}$ be Euler's pentagonal series in $\mathbb{Z}[[X]]$. If $p$ divides the coefficient of $X^{pm+r}$ in $E(X)^{p-1}$ for every natural number $m$, then $p$ divides the number of partitions of $pm + r$ for every natural number $m$.

results.title: Adèle ring of a field with respect to valuation subrings
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $F$ be a field, $P$ a type (of places) and, for each $p \in P$, let $O_p$ be a valuation subring of $F$. The adèle ring of $F$ with respect to $(O_p)_{p \in P}$ is the restricted product of the copies of $F$ with respect to the subrings $O_p$: its elements are the families $(a_p)_{p \in P}$ with $a_p \in F$ for every $p$ and $a_p \in O_p$ for all but finitely many $p$.

results.title: Extensionality for restricted-product adèles
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $F$ be a field, $P$ a type and, for each $p \in P$, let $O_p$ be a valuation subring of $F$. If two adèles $a$ and $b$ of the adèle ring of $F$ with respect to $(O_p)_{p \in P}$ satisfy $a_p = b_p$ for every $p \in P$, then $a = b$.

results.title: Adèles are integral at almost all places
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $F$ be a field, $P$ a type and, for each $p \in P$, let $O_p$ be a valuation subring of $F$. For every adèle $a$ of the adèle ring of $F$ with respect to $(O_p)_{p \in P}$, the component $a_p$ lies in $O_p$ for all but finitely many $p \in P$.

results.title: Increasing subsequence ending at a position
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $f : \{0, \dots, N-1\} \to \mathbb{R}$, a position $p$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$, this is the statement that $k \ge 1$ and $f$ has an increasing subsequence $\varphi$ of length $k$ (indices and values strictly increasing) ending at $p$, that is, with $\varphi(k-1) = p$.

results.title: Decreasing subsequence ending at a position
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $f : \{0, \dots, N-1\} \to \mathbb{R}$, a position $p$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$, this is the statement that $k \ge 1$ and $f$ has a decreasing subsequence $\varphi$ of length $k$ (indices strictly increasing and values strictly decreasing) ending at $p$, that is, with $\varphi(k-1) = p$.

results.title: No strict pair in a one-element set
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There are no $i, j \in \{0\}$ with $i < j$.

results.title: One-term subsequences are increasing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every real sequence $f$ indexed by $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$ and every position $p$, the subsequence of length $1$ consisting of the term at position $p$ is a strictly increasing subsequence of $f$.

results.title: One-term subsequences are decreasing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every real sequence $f$ indexed by $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$ and every position $p$, the subsequence of length $1$ consisting of the term at position $p$ is a strictly decreasing subsequence of $f$.

results.title: Length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at a position
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $f : \{0, \dots, N-1\} \to \mathbb{R}$ and a position $p$, this is the largest $k \le N$ such that $f$ has an increasing subsequence of length $k$ ending at $p$, where indices and values both increase strictly.

results.title: Length of the longest decreasing subsequence ending at a point
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a real sequence $f$ indexed by $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$ and an index $p$, this is the largest $k$ such that $f$ has a strictly decreasing subsequence of length $k$ ending at $p$, that is, indices $i_1 < \dots < i_k = p$ with $f(i_1) > \dots > f(i_k)$. The maximum exists: $k = 1$ qualifies, and every such $k$ is at most $N$.

results.title: Subsequences are no longer than the sequence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $\varphi \colon \{0, \dots, k-1\} \to \{0, \dots, N-1\}$ is strictly increasing, that is $\varphi(i) < \varphi(j)$ whenever $i < j$, then $k \le N$.

results.title: The longest increasing subsequence ending at a position is attained
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $f : \{0, \dots, N-1\} \to \mathbb{R}$ and every position $p$, $f$ has an increasing subsequence ending at $p$ whose length equals the length of the longest increasing subsequence of $f$ ending at $p$.

results.title: The longest decreasing subsequence ending at a point is attained
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every real sequence $f$ indexed by $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$ and every index $p$, $f$ has a strictly decreasing subsequence ending at $p$ whose length equals the length of the longest strictly decreasing subsequence of $f$ ending at $p$.

results.title: Bound by the longest increasing subsequence ending at a position
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f$ be a real sequence indexed by $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$ and let $p$ be a position. If $f$ has a strictly increasing subsequence of length $k$ ending exactly at $p$, then $k$ is at most the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence of $f$ ending at $p$.

results.title: Bound by the longest decreasing subsequence ending at a position
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f$ be a real sequence indexed by $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$ and let $p$ be a position. If $f$ has a strictly decreasing subsequence of length $k$ ending exactly at $p$, then $k$ is at most the length of the longest strictly decreasing subsequence of $f$ ending at $p$.

results.title: Longest increasing subsequences ending at a position have length at least one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $f : \{0, \dots, N-1\} \to \mathbb{R}$ and every position $p$, the length of the longest increasing subsequence of $f$ ending at $p$ is at least $1$.

results.title: The longest decreasing subsequence ending at a point has length at least one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every real sequence $f$ indexed by $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$ and every index $p$, the length of the longest strictly decreasing subsequence of $f$ ending at $p$ is at least $1$.

results.title: Appending an entry to a map of indices
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given $\varphi : \{0, \dots, k-1\} \to \{0, \dots, N-1\}$ and $p \in \{0, \dots, N-1\}$, the appended map on $\{0, \dots, k\}$ sends each $i < k$ to $\varphi(i)$ and sends $k$ to $p$.

results.title: Entries of a strictly increasing index map lie at or below its last entry
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $k \ge 1$ and let $\varphi : \{0, \dots, k-1\} \to \{0, \dots, N-1\}$ be strictly increasing with $\varphi(k-1) = q$. Then $\varphi(i) \le q$ for every $i < k$.

results.title: The last value is the largest along a strictly increasing selection
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f$ be a real sequence indexed by $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$, let $k \ge 1$, and let $\varphi$ map $\{0, \dots, k-1\}$ to $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$ so that $f(\varphi(i)) < f(\varphi(j))$ whenever $i < j < k$. If $\varphi(k-1) = q$, then $f(\varphi(i)) \le f(q)$ for every $i < k$.

results.title: The last value is the smallest along a strictly decreasing selection
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f$ be a real sequence indexed by $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$, let $k \ge 1$, and let $\varphi$ map $\{0, \dots, k-1\}$ to $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$ so that $f(\varphi(j)) < f(\varphi(i))$ whenever $i < j < k$. If $\varphi(k-1) = q$, then $f(q) \le f(\varphi(i))$ for every $i < k$.

results.title: Appending a later index keeps indices increasing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $k \ge 1$ and let $\varphi : \{0, \dots, k-1\} \to \{0, \dots, N-1\}$ be strictly increasing with last value $\varphi(k-1) = q$. If $p$ is an index with $q < p$, then the map on $\{0, \dots, k\}$ obtained by appending $p$ to $\varphi$, which sends each $i < k$ to $\varphi(i)$ and sends $k$ to $p$, is strictly increasing.

results.title: The last entry of an appended map
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every map $\varphi : \{0, \dots, k-1\} \to \{0, \dots, N-1\}$ and every $p \in \{0, \dots, N-1\}$, the map obtained by appending $p$ to $\varphi$ takes the value $p$ at its last index $k$.

results.title: Extending an increasing subsequence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f : \{0, \dots, N-1\} \to \mathbb{R}$, let $k \ge 1$, and let $\varphi$ be an increasing subsequence of $f$ of length $k$ (indices and values strictly increasing) with last index $\varphi(k-1) = q$. If $p \in \{0, \dots, N-1\}$ satisfies $q < p$ and $f(q) < f(p)$, then $f$ has an increasing subsequence of length $k + 1$ ending at $p$.

results.title: Extending a decreasing subsequence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f$ be a real sequence indexed by $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$, let $k \ge 1$, and let $\varphi$ be a decreasing subsequence of $f$ of length $k$, that is, indices $\varphi(0) < \dots < \varphi(k-1)$ with $f(\varphi(0)) > \dots > f(\varphi(k-1))$, whose last index is $\varphi(k-1) = q$. If $p$ is an index with $q < p$ and $f(p) < f(q)$, then $f$ has a decreasing subsequence of length $k + 1$ that ends at $p$.

results.title: Longest increasing subsequence lengths increase strictly along increasing pairs
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f : \{0, \dots, N-1\} \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $q < p$ be positions with $f(q) < f(p)$. Then the length of the longest increasing subsequence of $f$ ending at $q$ is strictly less than the length of the longest increasing subsequence of $f$ ending at $p$.

results.title: Longest decreasing subsequence lengths grow along a descent
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f$ be a real sequence indexed by $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$, and let $q < p$ be indices with $f(p) < f(q)$. Then the length of the longest strictly decreasing subsequence of $f$ ending at $q$ is strictly less than the length of the longest strictly decreasing subsequence of $f$ ending at $p$.

results.title: Increasing subsequences of every smaller length
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f$ be a real sequence indexed by $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$. If $f$ has a strictly increasing subsequence of length $k$, then for every $r \le k$ it has a strictly increasing subsequence of length $r$.

results.title: Decreasing subsequences of every smaller length
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f$ be a real sequence indexed by $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$. If $f$ has a strictly decreasing subsequence of length $k$, then for every $s \le k$ it has a strictly decreasing subsequence of length $s$.

results.title: Erdős–Szekeres theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $r, s \ge 1$ be natural numbers, let $N = (r - 1)(s - 1) + 1$, and let $f$ be an injective real sequence indexed by $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$. Then $f$ has a strictly increasing subsequence of length $r$, that is, indices $i_1 < \dots < i_r$ with $f(i_1) < \dots < f(i_r)$, or a strictly decreasing subsequence of length $s$, that is, indices $j_1 < \dots < j_s$ with $f(j_1) > \dots > f(j_s)$.

results.title: Legal moves in Sylver Coinage
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a set $M$ of natural numbers (a position of Sylver Coinage), the set $L(M)$ of legal moves consists of the natural numbers that are not finite sums of elements of $M$, repetitions allowed, i.e. the natural numbers outside the additive submonoid of $\mathbb{N}$ generated by $M$. Since $0$ is the empty sum, every legal move is positive.

results.title: P-positions of Sylver Coinage
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: A set $M$ of natural numbers is a P-position of Sylver Coinage when $1 \notin M$ and, for every legal move $q$ of $M$, the position $M \cup \{q\}$ is an N-position. P-positions and N-positions are defined together, as a mutual inductive definition. In particular a position whose only legal move is $1$ is a P-position (the player to move must name $1$ and loses).

results.title: N-positions of Sylver Coinage
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: A position $M$ of Sylver Coinage is an N-position (the player to move wins) when either $1 \in M$, so that the previous player named $1$ and lost, or some legal move $q$ of $M$ leads to a P-position $M \cup \{q\}$. N-positions and P-positions are defined together inductively by these rules.

results.title: Zero is never a legal move
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every set $M$ of natural numbers, $0$ is not a legal move of the Sylver Coinage position $M$.

results.title: The position $\{2, 3\}$ is a P-position
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In Sylver Coinage, the position $\{2, 3\}$ is a P-position: its only legal move is $1$.

results.title: Opening with 2 loses
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The position $\{2\}$ of Sylver Coinage is an N-position: the player to move wins by naming $3$, which leaves the P-position $\{2, 3\}$.

results.title: Hutchings' theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every prime $p > 3$, the position $\{p\}$ of Sylver Coinage is a P-position: a first player who opens with $p$ wins.

results.title: Ends of a Sylver Coinage position
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $M$ be a position of Sylver Coinage with set of legal moves $L(M)$. A natural number $x$ is an end of $M$ if $x \in L(M)$ and every $y \in L(M)$ with $y \ne x$ is still a legal move of the position $M \cup \{x\}$; that is, naming $x$ eliminates no other legal move.

results.title: The largest legal move is an end
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a position of Sylver Coinage whose set of legal moves $L(M)$ has a greatest element $F$. Then $F$ is an end of $M$.

results.title: In an ender, every smaller move eliminates the largest legal move
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a set of natural numbers whose set of legal moves $L(M)$ has a greatest element $F > 1$, and suppose that $F$ is the only end of $M$ (so $M$ is an ender). Then for every legal move $x$ of $M$ with $x < F$, the number $F$ is not a legal move of $M \cup \{x\}$.

results.title: Enders with largest legal move above 1 are N-positions
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a position of Sylver Coinage whose set of legal moves $L(M)$ has a greatest element $F$ with $F > 1$. If every end of $M$ equals $F$ (that is, $M$ is an ender), then $M$ is an N-position.

results.title: Two-generated numerical semigroups are symmetric
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a$, $b$ and $F$ be natural numbers and let $S = \langle a, b \rangle$ be the additive submonoid of $\mathbb{N}$ generated by $a$ and $b$. If $F \notin S$ and every natural number $n > F$ lies in $S$ (so $F$ is the Frobenius number of $S$), then $x \in S \iff F - x \notin S$ for every natural number $x \le F$.

results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a finite set of natural numbers whose set of legal moves $L(M)$ is finite, and suppose that removing any element changes the legal moves: $L(M \setminus \{a\}) \ne L(M)$ for every $a \in M$. Let $S$ be the additive submonoid of $\mathbb{N}$ generated by $M$. Then $M$ is the set of nonzero elements $s \in S$ such that whenever $s = a + b$ with $a, b \in S$, one of $a$ and $b$ is $0$; that is, $M$ is the…

results.title: Even replies to 4 and an odd number at least 5 lose
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x \ge 5$ be an odd natural number. For every even legal move $b$ of the position $\{4, x\}$, the position $\{4, x, b\}$ is an N-position.

results.title: Sicherman's claim on replies to 4 and an odd number
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every odd natural number $x \ge 5$ there is exactly one legal move $q$ of the position $\{4, x\}$ such that $\{4, x, q\}$ is a P-position, and every legal move $q$ of $\{4, x\}$ with $\{4, x, q\}$ a P-position satisfies $q \equiv x - 2 \pmod 4$.

results.title: Odd numbers above 3 have a unique odd partner after 4
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every odd natural number $q > 3$ there is exactly one odd natural number $x$ such that $\{4, x\}$ is an N-position and $\{4, x, q\}$ is a P-position.

results.title: Unique odd partner after 4
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $q > 3$ be an odd natural number. Then $\{4, q\}$ is an N-position of Sylver Coinage, and there is a unique odd natural number $x_q$ such that $\{4, x_q\}$ is an N-position and $\{4, q, x_q\}$ is a P-position.

results.title: Conway's bounds for 4-pairs
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $q$ and $x$ be odd natural numbers with $7 < q < x$ such that $\{4, x\}$ is an N-position and $\{4, x, q\}$ is a P-position of Sylver Coinage. Then $2q < x < 3q$.

results.title: Four-element P-positions containing 4
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x > 1$ be a natural number. If $x \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, then $\{4, x, x + 2, 6\}$ is a P-position; if $x \equiv 7 \pmod 8$, then $\{4, x, x + 2, 10\}$ is a P-position; if $x \equiv 5 \pmod 8$, then $\{4, x, x + 6, 10\}$ is a P-position; and if $x \equiv 1 \pmod 8$, then $\{4, x, x + 6, 14\}$ is a P-position.

results.title: Merging two blocks of a block-size list
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Merge the blocks at positions `i < j` of the block-size list `b`: remove both and append a block of size `b[i] + b[j]`.

results.title: Unordered pairs of blocks
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The unordered pairs of positions `i < j` among `k` blocks.

results.title: Random-joining law on block-size lists
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The random-joining law: `randomJoining m b ps` is the probability that `m` steps of random joining started from the block-size list `b` visit the list of block-size lists `ps` (starting with `b` itself). Each step merges a pair of blocks chosen uniformly among all pairs; the process stops once fewer than two blocks remain.

results.title: Transition operator of random joining
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The transition operator of random joining acting on a statistic `g` of block-size lists: the average of `g` over the lists obtained from `b` by merging a uniformly chosen pair of blocks (`g []` once fewer than two blocks remain). By `exists_finset_randomJoining`, its `j`-th iterate at `b` is the expectation of `g` at step `j` of random joining started from `b`.

results.title: Total branch length subtending i sample copies
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The total length of the branches subtending exactly `i` of the `n` sample copies, for the block-size history `ps` (entry `n - k` lists the block sizes while there are `k` lineages) and holding times `T`: `∑_{k=2}^{n} #{blocks of size i among k} · T k`.

results.title: Random joining has finite support and iterates the join step
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The random-joining law has finite support, and the expectation of a statistic of the `j`-th visited list (`j ≤ m`) is the `j`-th iterate of `joinStep`.

results.title: Expected number of blocks of size `i`
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Expected number of blocks of size `i` when `k` blocks remain, for random joining started from `n` singletons: `k · C(n-i-1, k-2) / C(n-1, k-1)` (Fu 1995; Griffiths–Tavaré 1998). Equivalently, a given one of the `k` blocks has size `i` with probability `C(n-i-1, k-2) / C(n-1, k-1)`.

results.title: Expected block counts weighted by coalescence times sum to $2/i$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Summing the expected block counts against `E T_k = (k.choose 2)⁻¹` gives `2 / i`: `∑_{k=2}^{n} k C(n-i-1, k-2) / C(n-1, k-1) · (k.choose 2)⁻¹ = 2 / i` for `1 ≤ i < n`.

results.title: Poisson likelihood of an observed count
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The Poisson likelihood `e^{-μ} μ^o / (o!)` of an observed count `o` at mean `μ`.

results.title: Positivity of the Poisson likelihood
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The likelihood is positive at a positive mean.

results.title: Flat-prior posterior of `γ`
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The likelihood `γ ↦ P(o | Poisson(γ E))` times `E` is the Gamma density of shape `o + 1` and rate `E`. For `E > 0` that density integrates to one, so `E` is the normalizing constant of the flat-prior posterior (the identity itself is algebraic and holds for every real `E`).

results.title: Upper confidence bound for the observed/expected ratio
results.caption: Definition

results.title: LOEUF
results.caption: Definition

results.title: The flat-prior posterior quantile is Garwood's bound
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The Gamma(`o + 1`, `E`) posterior puts mass exactly `1 - α` below `oeUpper α E o`.

results.title: Exact coverage
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every true ratio `γ ≥ 0` and `E > 0`, when `o ~ Poisson(γ E)`, `P(γ ≤ oeUpper α E o) ≥ 1 - α`.

results.title: Observed/expected upper bound with no observed variants

results.title: Observed/expected upper bound increases with the observed count

results.title: Observed/expected upper bound decreases with the expected count
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Posterior class probability in the Poisson mixture
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The posterior probability of class `c` for a gene with `o` observed and `E` expected LoF variants, in the Poisson mixture with prior weights `w` and class rates `rate`: `w_c P(o | rate_c E) / ∑_{c'} w_{c'} P(o | rate_{c'} E)`. pLI is this at the class with the smallest rate.
